guide.title: Putnam, Connecticut: Mill Town Turned Antiques Capital
guide.intro: Putnam was originally known as Aspinock and was incorporated in 1855 from sections of Killingly, Pomfret, and Thompson, taking its name from Revolutionary War hero General Israel Putnam. The Quinebaug River powered the town's growth: grist and saw mills served local farmers through the mid-1700s, and by incorporation several large cotton mills lined the river alongside a new rail line. In August 1955, hurricanes Connie and Diane brought torrential rain across Connecticut within a week of each other; the resulting flood destroyed homes, businesses, and factories in Putnam and washed away the railroad bed, accelerating the decline of the town's mill economy. Putnam reinvented itself by filling its empty mills with antique dealers, and beginning in the early 2000s many of those shops gave way to restaurants and a walkable Main Street arts district — the character the town keeps today.

sections.heading: From Aspinock to antiques
sections.body: The land along the Quinebaug River was first developed by grist and saw mills serving local farms in the mid-1700s. By 1855, when the town incorporated as Putnam — named for Revolutionary War hero General Israel Putnam — cotton mills and a rail line had already arrived, and the town became a manufacturing center supplying goods for Civil War soldiers. That mill economy ended abruptly in August 1955, when hurricanes Connie and Diane dropped heavy rain across Connecticut within a week of each other; the resulting flood destroyed homes, businesses, and factories in Putnam and washed away the railroad bed. The town's empty mill buildings found a second life as an antiques center, and beginning in the early 2000s many antique shops were replaced by restaurants and a small arts community — the walkable Main Street that visitors find today. Textile executive George Morse's mansion and the River Mills Heritage Trail, which interprets six former factory sites, still trace that manufacturing past.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Putnam is a drive-to destination in the Quiet Corner: Interstate 395 is the main north-south corridor through town, and US Route 44 is the principal east-west route, with Routes 12, 21, and 171 feeding Main Street. There is no passenger rail station in Putnam. The nearest rail service is Union Station in Worcester, Massachusetts, about 30 miles north, with Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited and MBTA commuter rail to Boston; New London Union Station, about 45 miles south, offers Amtrak Northeast Regional trains and CTrail Shore Line East. The Northeastern Connecticut Transit District runs local bus service connecting Putnam to ten other Quiet Corner towns.

sections.heading: Where to eat and stay
sections.body: Downtown Putnam's Main Street carries the town's dining, from 85 Main's lunch and dinner specials to Blackstone Putnam's land-and-sea flights, Courthouse Bar & Grille's burgers and steaks, and Bear Hands Brewing's taproom of house beers and ciders. Putnam has no hotel, inn, or B&B of its own; the closest confirmed options are the Inn at Woodstock Hill, about seven miles west in neighboring Woodstock, and the Quiet Corner Inn in Brooklyn.

faq.question: How do I get to Putnam?
faq.answer: By car — Interstate 395 is the main north-south corridor, and US Route 44 the principal east-west route, with Routes 12, 21, and 171 feeding Main Street. There is no passenger rail station in Putnam; the nearest rail service is in Worcester, MA (about 30 miles north) or New London Union Station (about 45 miles south).

faq.question: Why is Putnam known for antiques?
faq.answer: After the town's textile mills declined, empty mill buildings were filled with antique dealers. Beginning in the early 2000s many of those shops gave way to restaurants and a small arts community along Main Street.

faq.question: What happened to Putnam in 1955?
faq.answer: Hurricanes Connie and Diane brought heavy rain to Connecticut within a week of each other that August; the resulting flood destroyed homes, businesses, and factories in Putnam and washed away the railroad bed.

faq.question: Is there a train to Putnam?
faq.answer: No — there is no passenger rail station in Putnam. The nearest rail service is Union Station in Worcester, Massachusetts (about 30 miles north) or New London Union Station (about 45 miles south).

faq.question: Where can I stay near Putnam?
faq.answer: Putnam has no hotel, inn, or B&B of its own. The closest confirmed options are the Inn at Woodstock Hill, about seven miles west in neighboring Woodstock, and the Quiet Corner Inn in Brooklyn.

places.name: The Bradley Playhouse
places.summary: A former vaudeville theater in downtown Putnam, now home to a local performing arts company staging a full season of plays and musicals.

places.name: Putnam River Trail
places.address: Trailhead parking along Kennedy Drive, Putnam, CT 06260
places.summary: A paved 2.7-mile multi-use path along the Quinebaug River, built in 1998 and extended in 2009 and 2016, with five parking areas and five bridges offering river views.

places.name: The Complex Performing & Creative Arts Centre
places.summary: A Main Street arts school offering dance, theatre, music and creative arts through an interdisciplinary curriculum, organized into age bands of roughly 3-6, 6-8, 8-10, 11-15 and 15-18 and five development levels from Emerging Artists to Advanced Artists. It runs a Conservatory Program, arts education programs and artist residencies, and its student companies are The Complex Dance Company, The Performance Company and NECT Ballet Company, alongside a chapter of the National Honor Society for Dance Arts.

places.name: Aspinock Historical Society of Putnam
places.address: Suite 250, Putnam Municipal Complex, 200 School St., Putnam, CT 06260
places.summary: Founded in 1972, this nonprofit runs a research center and museum of Putnam's mill-town history, with re-enactors, lectures, and community tours. Open Tuesday-Thursday, 10 a.m.-2 p.m., and Saturdays by appointment.

places.name: 85 Main
places.summary: A Main Street restaurant with a private event space called The Cellar, taking reservations and online orders and running lunch and dinner specials.

places.name: Blackstone Putnam
places.summary: A restaurant at 35 Main Street built around a 'flight' concept: shareable sets of three, including land-and-sea flights of filet, wagyu, ribeye, lobster and scallops, food flights of egg rolls, sliders, bruschetta, truffle fries and mac and cheese, and espresso martini and cocktail flights. Open daily 11am to 9pm, and to 11pm on Friday and Saturday.

places.name: Courthouse Bar & Grille
places.summary: A Main Street pub-restaurant serving burgers, wraps and sandwiches, steaks, seafood and pasta, with sixteen rotating draft taps, seasonal and signature cocktails and a wine list. It runs a weekly 'Tito's Tuesdays' promotion, and posts hours of Sunday to Thursday 11:30am to 10pm and Friday and Saturday 11:30am to midnight.

places.name: Bear Hands Brewing Company
places.summary: A downtown brewery and taproom at 75 Main Street, pouring around eleven house beers plus hard cider and spirits — Key Lime Pie gose, SMPLFD hefeweizen, Show Me Sabro and Mango Habanero New England IPAs, Sanity Pils, Pillow Fighting With Chairs double IPA, Mind Fack golden mocha stout, Brown Bag'n It American porter and a rose cider among them. By its own account the brewery took about three years of work to open.
